cfb7095add:
The first problem is carrying data around. A plain class forces you to hand-write __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for every record type in your program. That is mechanical work, and mechanical work breeds copy-paste bugs.

Dictionaries from JSON have the opposite problem: no shape at all. A dict arriving from an API could hold anything. Nothing in your code says what you expect.
a15b23474d: Part A covers the data carriers: dataclasses, TypedDict, NamedTuple, and Protocol, and how to pick between them. Part B covers type hints. It explains what annotations mean, how generics and unions work, and how a static checker reads the labels Python skips.
cc52e7f069: The @dataclass decorator (PEP 557, docs) is a code generator. At class-creation time it reads the annotated attributes of your class. Then it writes __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ into the class for you. You declare the fields; it writes the machinery.
1fe6fb8e62: The manual PointOld needs fifteen lines to do what the two-line dataclass does. The decorator version behaves exactly the same. The generated __init__ takes x and y positionally or by keyword, just as if you wrote it.
918392cf07: Reach for dataclasses when a class mostly carries data: rows, messages, configs, results. Skip them when construction needs genuinely custom logic. In that case, write __init__ yourself instead of fighting __post_init__. And when the class is mostly behavior with a little state, a plain class reads more honestly.
fc2fd4eadc: Fields take defaults like function parameters. Mutable defaults, though, are banned outright; the next section explains why. For a fresh mutable value per instance, use field(default_factory=list). The factory is a zero-argument callable, called once per new instance.
02d8d532bf:
Two more field() options matter daily:

  • field(init=False) excludes the field from the generated __init__. Use it for values you compute rather than receive.
  • field(repr=False) hides a noisy field from the repr without removing it.
75737559d3: One ordering rule bites everyone once. Fields without defaults cannot follow fields with defaults, the same as function parameters. Put name: str after price: float = 0.0 and the class definition raises TypeError: non-default argument 'name' follows default argument.
03e0460358: The default value in a class body is evaluated once, when the class is created. If Python allowed = [], every instance would share one list. Appending to one order's tags would corrupt every other order. This is the same rule as mutable function defaults, applied one level up. Python chose a loud error over a silent aliasing bug. Good trade.
670c38e2df:
The fix is field(default_factory=list): pass the callable, not a value. Each instance calls list() and gets its own.

The classic mistake is field(default_factory=[]), which passes an instance instead of a callable. That one doesn't fail at class definition. It fails later, at instantiation, with the confusing TypeError: 'list' object is not callable. When you see that error, check your default_factory arguments first.
2575f04501:
Second, and more important: frozen is shallow. It locks the bindings, meaning which object each attribute name points to. It does not lock the objects themselves. The frozen Holder still holds a live, mutable list. Freezing the box doesn't freeze what's inside the box.

If you need deep immutability, use immutable contents: tuples instead of lists, and MappingProxyType instead of dicts (Task A3 shows the pattern).
b1b4003695:
Freezing comes with one bonus. A frozen dataclass with eq=True (the default) gets a generated __hash__, so instances work as dict keys and in sets.

Non-frozen dataclasses are unhashable by default: eq=True sets __hash__ to None. The reason is safety. A mutable object that changes its hash while sitting in a set would corrupt the set.
912e64cfc0: Reach for frozen=True for value objects: points, money amounts, config snapshots. It fits anything where identity comes from the values and mutation would be a bug. The reason to prefer it isn't philosophy. Frozen objects are safe to share between threads, safe as dict keys, and safe to pass around without defensive copies.
f5d3394e41: Try it — Task A3. A frozen Settings dataclass holds values: dict. Freezing doesn't stop callers from mutating the dict. Fix it in __post_init__: wrap the dict in types.MappingProxyType (a read-only view). Assign it with object.__setattr__, the sanctioned escape hatch inside __post_init__. Verify that both s.values["k"] = v and s.values = {} are rejected. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
1a0104e432:
order=True generates the comparison methods <, <=, >, and >=. They compare fields as a tuple, in declaration order. Sorting a list of versions just works.

It requires eq=True (the default). Combining order=True with eq=False raises ValueError: eq must be true if order is true at class definition.
5e6d055bf4:
slots=True removes the per-instance __dict__. Instances use less memory and attribute access gets slightly faster. The trade: instances can no longer grow new attributes, and they lose weak-reference support.

Under the hood the decorator builds a brand-new class with __slots__. This flag changes more machinery than the others, so reach for it deliberately. It suits many small short-lived objects. Don't use it by default.
5198fea584: TypedDict (PEP 589, in the typing module) describes a dictionary's shape for static checkers. You declare the keys and their value types. At runtime it is still a plain dict. The shape exists for readers and checkers, not for the interpreter.
c78fa405d5: By default every key is required. total=False flips the default so every key is optional. Then Required[...] marks the exceptions back. Required and NotRequired (available since Python 3.11) let you mix required and optional keys precisely. TypedDicts also compose through inheritance, which keeps shared key sets in one place.
b199cbbb4b: Try it — Task A2. Model a weather API response as a Weather TypedDict. It has required city: str and temp_c: float, plus optional humidity: int and wind_kph: float via NotRequired. Write a summarize(w: Weather) -> str function. It should print what's present without KeyError on what's absent. Then extend it with a Forecast(Weather) subclass adding an optional chance_of_rain. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
24665e6af5: If you need bad data rejected when it arrives, that is runtime validation, and it takes a different tool. Pydantic, a third-party library, validates at runtime and raises on bad input. That is genuinely useful at system boundaries. It is also genuinely not what TypedDict does. Confusing the two leads to trusting data you never checked.
058c467ae6:
The selection logic in words starts with ownership.

  • If the data arrives from outside (JSON, a config file, another service) and its shape is known, that's a TypedDict. You don't own it, so you describe it rather than model it.
  • If the data is yours, such as an internal record you construct and pass around, that's a dataclass. It gives you defaults, validation, and methods.

The other three are specializations. A plain dict is for genuinely schemaless data: a bag of user-supplied options, a JSON blob you forward untouched. A NamedTuple is for records so small they'd drown in a class body. It stays a real tuple, so unpacking and indexing keep working:
017afcf558: The most common real-world mistake is reaching for a dataclass for API responses. It feels tidy: objects instead of dicts. But the API owns that shape, and its keys will drift. Describe the boundary with a TypedDict and convert to your own dataclass once inside. Then the drift stays contained in one conversion function.
e5fa1b1c50:
This one example teaches three lessons.

  1. First, add("2", "3") returns "23" (string concatenation) with zero complaint. The annotations are documentation the interpreter files away.
  2. Second, add.__annotations__ shows where they live. It is a plain dict on the function object, with keys for each parameter plus 'return'.
  3. Third, count: int creates nothing. A bare annotation without assignment is a label with no jar. Accessing count raises NameError, exactly as if the line weren't there.
91a8d31981:
One more evaluation detail, because it bites. As of Python 3.13, annotations are evaluated eagerly when the def statement runs. Annotating a parameter with a name that doesn't exist yet raises NameError at definition time.

Sometimes you need forward references, such as annotating with a class defined later in the file. For those, add from __future__ import annotations at the top. It stores every annotation as an unevaluated string.
acec2a5558:
list alone says "a list of something." list[int] says "a list of ints." That's a generic type: a type parameterized by another type.

Since Python 3.9 (PEP 585), the built-in collections accept parameters directly: list[int], dict[str, float], tuple[str, int], set[str]. The old typing.List[int] spelling still works. But the builtin spelling is shorter, and there is no reason to prefer the old one in new code.
c06f95bcee: Common mistakes here are version-shaped. int | str in an annotation on Python 3.9 raises TypeError, because the | syntax needs 3.10+. On this guide's Python 3.13 both spellings work. Code you share with 3.9 users, though, needs typing.Union or typing.Optional. Know your floor.
918fbd32a8: Try it — Task B1. Write a retry helper. It takes a zero-argument callable fn, calls it up to attempts times, and returns whatever fn returns. Annotate it with Callable[[], T] and a TypeVar, so the return type follows the callable's return type. Add a log: Literal["silent", "warn"] parameter. When set to "warn", it prints each failure. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
b2dba1bb74:
A TypeVar lets a function stay generic without lying. def first(items: list[T]) -> T says: "whatever the element type is, that's what I return." Call it with list[int] and you get int back. Call it with list[str] and you get str.

The classic spelling declares T = TypeVar("T") first. Since Python 3.12, PEP 695 lets you write the type parameter directly on the function: def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T. Both work on 3.13. The new spelling is shorter; the old one works on older Pythons.
8db84a837d: Protocol (PEP 544) is structural typing: duck typing with a signature. Normal inheritance is nominal typing. A class is a Reader because it says class File(Reader). A Protocol works differently. A class is Readable if it has a read() method returning str, whether or not it ever heard of Readable. The checker verifies the structure, not the lineage.
6ba582b36d: So when should you use a Protocol over an abstract base class? Use one when the types you accept come from different libraries, or from code you don't control, and you can't make them all inherit from one base. When you do control the hierarchy, an ABC with shared implementation is usually simpler. A Protocol describes; an ABC provides.
17876c06b5:
Any tells the checker to look away. Every operation on an Any value passes silently, whether attribute access, calls, or arithmetic. The checker assumes you know what you're doing.

object, the true top of the type hierarchy, tells the checker the truth. This could be anything, so you may do nothing with it until you narrow it down with isinstance. Any disables checking; object invites it.
31aa58850e: The runtime behavior is identical. Both functions accept anything, because annotations never gate execution. The difference exists entirely in the checker's head. shout_any(42) blows up at runtime precisely because the checker was told not to look.
44918f0a4a:
The practical rule: Any belongs at the boundary where you genuinely cannot know the type. json.loads returns Any, and that's honest, because JSON really can hold anything.

But don't let Any travel. Narrow it with isinstance as close to the boundary as you can. This is called narrowing: inside the if branch, the checker tracks the type getting more precise. Annotate the rest of your code with what you actually use. A codebase where every other annotation is Any has paid the cost of annotating for none of the benefit.
85a36e5475:
mypy and pyright are third-party tools, not part of Python. Python ships no type checker, and the interpreter never consults your annotations. mypy installs via pip, pyright via npm. Both read your source files and report the inconsistencies your annotations reveal:

  • wrong argument types
  • assignments that contradict declarations
  • functions that return the wrong type
ff9e01ccd2: Neither tool is installed in this environment, so what follows is illustrative. It shows the shape of a real report, not a transcript of a real run. The Python execution, on the other hand, is real and was verified: annotations change nothing at runtime.
8f84ea1687: The checker caught what the interpreter couldn't: total was declared str but assigned an int. Python assigned happily. type(total) proves the annotation didn't convert anything. It's still an int wearing a str label.
659e0c103f:
Keep the mental model clean. The checker is a separate program with opinions, like a linter. It reads your code without running it. Python runs your code without reading the annotations. The two never meet.

The checker is not a phase of execution, and "my code is type-checked" never means "my code is type-safe at runtime." What type-checking buys you is earlier, cheaper discovery. It finds the mistakes that would have blown up at runtime, while you're still at your desk.
fab7695bf9: Annotations pay off gradually. Here's one function evolving. Each stage costs a little, and each stage buys something concrete.
49046b2bb5:
Stage 1 works and says nothing. A caller must read the body to learn that pct is a percentage, not a fraction.

Stage 2 documents the contract: floats in, float out. A reader now knows the shape, and so does the checker at every call site.

Stage 3 goes further. The coupon codes become a Literal, so a checker rejects discount3(100, "SAVE99") before it ever runs. The dict lookup that would have raised KeyError at runtime becomes a compile-time-style error at the call site.
dd6d309aed:
The deeper lesson is about where precision pays. Stage 2's annotations cost one line and help every reader. Stage 3's Literal costs a named alias and pays off everywhere the function is called.

Annotate the boundaries first: public functions, module APIs, the shapes crossing between components. Then annotate the tricky internals where the types aren't obvious. You don't need to annotate everything on day one. The function at stage 1 still runs. The annotations were always optional, and they're still optional. They're just useful.
c19c1ee348: The total property is derived, not stored. It needs no field(init=False), and it can't drift out of sync with unit_price or quantity.
951a3f156f: The "humidity" in w guard is the runtime counterpart of NotRequired. The checker knows the key may be absent, and the in check is how you respect that at runtime. A Forecast is a Weather with more keys, so summarize accepts it. TypedDict inheritance is substitutable this way.
1b92fc1bc1:
There are two layers of defense. MappingProxyType makes the contents read-only, so mutating raises TypeError. frozen=True makes the binding read-only, so rebinding raises FrozenInstanceError.

Note the annotation changed to Mapping. That's the honest type, since callers only get the read-only view. object.__setattr__ is the sanctioned way to set a field inside __post_init__ of a frozen dataclass. It's the one place the freeze is deliberately bypassable, during construction.
d75a3e0f29:
T is inferred per call: retry(flaky) returns str, and retry(lambda: 42) returns int. One annotation gives both call sites precise types.

The assert last_error is not None exists for the checker. After the loop, the checker can't prove the loop always raised, so the assert documents what you know. And Literal["silent", "warn"] means a typo like "quite" gets flagged before the function ever runs.
